items.prompt: How did a woolly mammoth's coat keep it warm through an ice-age winter?

options.label: A single layer of short fur trapped body heat close to the skin
options.feedback: A single short layer traps far less still air than a coat with two distinct layers working together; a mammoth's coat was built with more than that alone.

options.label: Long outer guard hairs shielded a dense underwool that trapped still air near the skin
options.feedback: Long, coarse guard hairs shed wind, rain, and snow, while a thick undercoat beneath them held a layer of still air against the skin, and still air is what actually holds warmth in.

options.label: Oily skin repelled the cold instead of hair
options.feedback: The insulation came from hair and fat, not from an oily skin surface; a mammoth's build relied on layers, not a coating.

options.label: The fur constantly grew warmer by producing its own heat
options.feedback: Hair itself produces no heat; it only traps the warmth the body itself is generating underneath it.

items.ok_line: An outer shield against wind, an inner layer that traps stillness.
items.ko_line: Think of two separate jobs — keeping weather out, and holding air still — done by two different kinds of hair.
items.exp_text: Long, coarse guard hairs formed an outer shield that turned aside wind, rain, and snow before it ever reached the skin. Underneath that shield grew a much denser layer of shorter, finer wool, and it was this underwool that trapped a layer of still air close to the body. Still air conducts heat away far more slowly than moving air does, so it was this trapped stillness, held in place by two different kinds of hair working together, that kept the animal's own body heat from escaping.

items.prompt: What did a woolly mammoth most likely use its long, curved tusks for in everyday life?

options.label: Sweeping snow aside to reach buried grass, and stripping bark from trees
options.feedback: Curved tusks swept low across the ground could push snow out of the way to expose grass beneath it, and the same tusks could pry or scrape bark away from a trunk.

options.label: Storing water for use during dry spells
options.feedback: A tusk is solid, dense material with no internal cavity built for holding liquid; it could not hold water at all.

options.label: Channelling sound to improve the animal's hearing
options.feedback: Hearing worked through the ears, as in any mammal; a solid tusk has no structure suited to gathering or channelling sound.

options.label: Filtering plant matter out of drinking water
options.feedback: Filtering structures would need fine gaps or bristles; a tusk's smooth, solid surface was not built for straining anything out of water.

items.ok_line: A curved tool for clearing snow and stripping bark, growing the whole time it was used.
items.ko_line: Think about what stands in the way of a mammoth's food in winter, and what a long curved tusk could do about it.
items.exp_title: A tool for reaching food under snow and bark
items.exp_text: A tusk was a greatly enlarged, continuously growing incisor tooth, curved so its tip could sweep low and to the side rather than pointing straight ahead. Swept across snow-covered ground, that curve could push snow aside and uncover the grass buried beneath it, and the same tusk could pry at bark or wedge into a branch to strip it. Growing throughout the animal's life the way it did, a tusk kept a working edge even as its tip wore down from constant use against snow, wood, and frozen ground.

items.prompt: How did a woolly rhinoceros most likely use the large, flattened horn on its snout?

options.label: As a hollow chamber for storing extra body fat
options.feedback: A horn like this is made of solid, compacted material similar to hair, not a hollow chamber; fat was stored elsewhere in the body.

options.label: As a sweeping tool to clear snow away from frozen vegetation
options.feedback: A broad, flattened horn dragged low across the ground could push snow to one side, uncovering the tough grasses growing underneath it.

options.label: As a paddle for swimming across rivers
options.feedback: Nothing about a solid horn fixed rigidly to the snout suits paddling through water; its flattened shape instead matches sweeping motion across the ground.

options.label: As a resonating chamber to deepen the animal's call
options.feedback: Sound production in a mammal comes from the throat and airway, not from a solid horn made of compacted hair-like fibre.

items.ok_line: A flattened blade for pushing snow off the grass beneath it.
items.ko_line: Picture the horn's shape — broad and flat — and think what that shape does well against snow.
items.exp_title: A flattened blade against the snow
items.exp_text: The horn was compressed side to side into a broad, flattened shape rather than a rounded spike, and worn fossil horns show wear consistent with being dragged sideways along the ground. Swept low across a snow-covered field this way, the flattened edge could shift snow aside and expose the tough, frozen grass growing beneath it. A horn shaped and angled for sweeping rather than stabbing let the animal reach food that lay hidden under a covering it could not simply eat through.

items.prompt: How did the giant antlers of the Irish elk regrow to their full size again after being shed each year?

options.label: The old antlers were never actually shed at all
options.feedback: Antlers of this kind are shed and regrown on a yearly cycle, unlike the permanent horns of a species such as cattle.

options.label: New antlers grew slowly over several years before use
options.feedback: The growth happened within a single cycle each year, not stretched out gradually across several years before the antlers could be used.

options.label: A skin rich in blood vessels, called velvet, fed rapid new bone growth beneath it
options.feedback: Blood flowing through the soft velvet skin delivered the nutrients and minerals needed for the antler bone underneath to grow at a fast pace, before the velvet was shed once growth finished.

options.label: The antlers were made of the same material as tooth enamel
options.feedback: Antlers are made of true bone, grown and later shed, unlike tooth enamel, which is not regrown once it forms.

items.ok_line: A blood-rich skin feeding fast-growing bone, shed once the growing was done.
items.ko_line: Think about what covered a growing antler before it hardened, and what that covering carried.
items.exp_title: Bone grown fast under a living skin
items.exp_text: A growing antler was covered in a soft skin called velvet, threaded through with blood vessels that carried minerals and nutrients straight to the bone forming underneath. Fed this steadily, the antler could grow at a pace far faster than most bone growth elsewhere in the body, building up its full branching shape before the mating season it was needed for. Once growth finished and the bone hardened, blood flow to the velvet was cut off, and the elk rubbed the now-dead skin away to reveal bare antler beneath.

items.prompt: What can worn, polished patches on the floor of an ice-age cave, alongside deep claw marks on the walls, reveal about how cave bears used that cave?

options.label: That the cave was flooded regularly by an underground river
options.feedback: Smoothed floors and claw marks come from an animal's body moving repeatedly across stone, not from water passing through the cave.

options.label: That the bears never actually entered the cave itself
options.feedback: Wear patterns shaped like a resting body, alongside claw marks reachable only from inside, point to bears spending real time within the cave, not staying outside it.

options.label: That the cave was used only once, by a single passing bear
options.feedback: A single, brief visit would leave scattered scratches rather than floor stone smoothed down by repeated contact over a long span of time.

options.label: That the cave was used repeatedly, year after year, for sleeping through winter
options.feedback: A single visit could not smooth stone through wear, and scattered claw marks alone would not show a pattern; both point instead to the same spot being used again and again over many winters.

items.ok_line: Stone smoothed down by the same bodies returning, winter after winter.
items.ko_line: Ask what it takes to actually smooth solid rock: one visit, or many repeated ones.
items.exp_title: A den returned to, year after year
items.exp_text: Bare stone does not smooth itself; it takes the repeated pressure of bodies lying, turning, and rising in the same spot, again and again over a long span of time, to polish rock down the way these cave floors are polished. Claw marks scored deep into the walls at heights a bear could reach while standing or stretching tell the same story, made by animals returning to scratch and mark the same surfaces repeatedly rather than passing through just once. Together, the smoothed stone and the layered claw marks point to the same den being used through one winter after another.

items.prompt: How did dire wolves most likely bring down prey much larger than any single wolf?

options.label: By hunting and coordinating in a pack rather than alone
options.feedback: Wolves hunting together could surround, tire, and press a large animal from several sides at once, overwhelming prey that no lone hunter could have safely tackled.

options.label: By injecting venom through a bite to weaken prey
options.feedback: No wolf, living or extinct, delivers venom through a bite; a dire wolf's teeth and jaws worked through direct force alone.

options.label: By waiting for prey to die of old age before feeding
options.feedback: Worn and broken teeth found on dire wolf skeletons show heavy use consistent with active hunting, not with waiting for prey to simply die on its own.

options.label: By ambushing prey alone under cover of darkness
options.feedback: Bones found clustered together at shared feeding sites point to wolves gathering and feeding as a group, not to solitary ambush hunting.

items.ok_line: Numbers did what no single set of jaws could manage alone.
items.ko_line: Think about what several hunters working together can do that one alone cannot.
items.exp_text: A single wolf attacking prey many times its own size risks a kick or a gore that could disable or kill it outright, a risk that dropped sharply once several wolves closed in together from different sides. Working as a group let the pack tire large prey by harassing it from multiple directions at once, wearing down an animal that could otherwise simply outrun or overpower any one attacker alone. Fossil sites where the bones of many dire wolves are found clustered together around the remains of large prey point to exactly this kind of group effort at the kill.

items.prompt: How did huge herds of grazing mammals, such as mammoths and bison, help keep the ice-age grassland known as the mammoth steppe from turning into forest or moss-covered tundra?

options.label: By burning patches of vegetation with their body heat
options.feedback: No grazing animal generates heat capable of burning vegetation; grassland here was maintained by grazing and trampling, not by any heat given off by the herd.

options.label: By constantly cropping grass short and trampling down any young trees trying to take root
options.feedback: Grazing kept grass short and vigorous rather than letting it grow tall and woody, while hooves and feet trampling the same ground damaged tree seedlings before they could establish themselves.

options.label: By spreading a chemical through their saliva that killed young trees
options.feedback: No such chemical defence is known in the saliva of any grazing mammal; the effect on tree seedlings came from physical trampling, not from any substance in the mouth.

options.label: By digging deep burrows that destroyed tree roots underground
options.feedback: These were surface grazers, not diggers; their effect on the landscape came from grazing and trampling on the surface, not from burrowing below it.

items.ok_line: Grazed short and trampled flat, before any tree could get a foothold.
items.ko_line: Think about what large herds do to the ground simply by feeding and moving across it.
items.exp_title: A landscape shaped by feeding and trampling
items.exp_text: Grasses respond to being grazed by growing back low and dense from the base, while trees and shrubs need their young shoots to survive undisturbed for a long stretch of time before they can grow tall. Herds moving and feeding across the same ground cropped any such shoots down before they had the chance, and their hooves and feet further damaged seedlings simply by trampling the same paths over and over. Grazing pressure kept the balance tipped toward open grass rather than toward the woody growth that would otherwise have slowly closed the landscape in.

items.prompt: Why did woolly mammoths have noticeably smaller ears and shorter tails than their living elephant relatives in warmer climates?

options.label: Smaller ears and tails made the animal faster over snow
options.feedback: Speed depends mainly on the legs and overall build; ear and tail size have little effect on how fast an animal can move.

options.label: Smaller ears and tails weighed less, saving energy on migration
options.feedback: Ears and tails make up only a tiny fraction of an animal's total body weight; the difference in size is better explained by heat loss than by any meaningful saving in weight.

options.label: Smaller extremities lose less body heat to the cold surrounding air
options.feedback: A large, flat ear or a long tail exposes a lot of surface area to the air, and heat escapes fastest through exactly that kind of surface, so shrinking those parts helped hold body heat in.

options.label: Predators could not grab hold of smaller ears and tails
options.feedback: A body covered in thick fur already left little for a predator to grip; the size difference lines up instead with how much heat each body part loses in the cold.

items.ok_line: Less surface exposed to the cold, less warmth lost through it.
items.ko_line: Think about which parts of a body lose the most heat, simply because of their shape.
items.exp_text: Heat escapes a body fastest through parts with a lot of surface exposed to the air relative to how much flesh sits underneath, and a large, thin, flat ear or a long, thin tail are both shapes built almost entirely out of that kind of exposed surface. Shrinking those parts down cut back on the surface available for heat to escape through, while keeping the deeper body, packed with warm muscle and fat, largely unchanged in size. A cold-adapted body built this way traded a little reach and hearing range for a real advantage in holding onto its own warmth.

items.prompt: How did the teeth of an American mastodon differ from those of a woolly mammoth, matching a different way of feeding?

options.label: No teeth at all, since it fed by filtering water
options.feedback: A mastodon fed on solid plant matter using well-developed teeth; filtering through water belongs to entirely different kinds of animals.

options.label: Teeth made of the same flattened plates as a mammoth's, but larger
options.feedback: The two animals' teeth differed in shape, not simply in size; a mastodon's cone-shaped cusps matched a browsing diet quite unlike a mammoth's flat grinding ridges.

options.label: Teeth that never stopped growing throughout its life, unlike a mammoth's
options.feedback: Both animals' cheek teeth grew and were replaced in sets rather than growing continuously; the real difference between them lay in the shape of the chewing surface, not in continuous growth.

options.label: Cone-shaped cusps suited to crushing leaves and twigs, rather than flat ridges for grinding grass
options.feedback: Rows of pointed, cone-shaped cusps could puncture and crush the leaves, twigs, and cones a browsing animal fed on, a very different job from grinding down tough, gritty grass.

items.ok_line: Cusps for puncturing leaves, not ridges for milling grass.
items.ko_line: Think about the shape of the chewing surface needed for leaves and twigs, compared with the shape needed for grass.
items.exp_title: Teeth shaped for a different diet
items.exp_text: A mammoth's cheek teeth carried a series of tightly packed, flat ridges running across the tooth, a shape well suited to milling down tough, gritty, low-growing grass. A mastodon's teeth instead carried rows of separate, rounded cusps rising up from the tooth's surface, better suited to puncturing and crushing softer leaves, twigs, and cones from trees and shrubs. Two animals living in similar cold landscapes fed on quite different parts of the same plants because their teeth were shaped for two different jobs.

items.prompt: How did a warming climate at the end of the last ice age make life harder for large grazing animals like the woolly mammoth, beyond simply raising the temperature?

options.label: Open grassland increasingly gave way to forest and wetland, shrinking the grazing land these animals depended on
options.feedback: As the climate warmed, trees and shrubs spread into ground that had been open grassland, and the grasses these animals relied on for food became patchier and harder to find across a shrinking landscape.

options.label: Warmer air became too thin for these animals to breathe comfortably
options.feedback: Air near sea level does not thin out as temperature rises the way it does at high altitude; breathing was not the difficulty a warming climate created for these animals.

options.label: Warmer temperatures caused the animals' fur to fall out entirely within days
options.feedback: A coat adapted to cold would shed only gradually as a climate warmed over a long stretch of time, not vanish within days; the larger problem was the changing landscape itself, not the fur alone.

options.label: Rising temperatures melted the animals' tusks
options.feedback: Tusks are solid bone-like material, unaffected by temperatures far short of what would be needed to melt anything at all; the real threat from warming came through the landscape and food supply, not through the tusks directly.

items.ok_line: The grassland itself shrank away, long before any single animal did.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to open grassland, specifically, as a climate slowly warms.
items.exp_title: A shrinking grassland, not just a warmer one
items.exp_text: A warming climate favours the spread of trees, shrubs, and wetland plants into ground that had previously stayed open and dominated by grass, since those plants could now survive conditions that had once been too cold for them. As forest and wetland crept into the grassland's place, the food supply that vast grazing herds depended on grew patchier and had to be searched for across a wider area. A landscape changing shape under the animals' feet this way left large grazers competing for a shrinking share of the ground each still needed to survive.
